persona.name: Geeta Verma
persona.background: She works long hours in a small tailoring shop and recently had a period of poor appetite and weight loss, making it harder to keep up with work.

diagnoses.name: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia
diagnoses.description: Common HIV-associated pneumonia with subacute fever, dyspnea, nonproductive cough, hypoxemia and often bilateral perihilar diffuse symmetric interstitial pattern or CT ground-glass opacities; typically with CD4 <200.

diagnoses.name: Pulmonary tuberculosis
diagnoses.description: AIDS-defining condition that can occur at any CD4 count; can present with cough and dyspnea and is suggested when symptoms have been present for several weeks or fail to respond to standard antibiotics.

diagnoses.name: Community-acquired pneumococcal pneumonia (Streptococcus pneumoniae)
diagnoses.description: Bacterial pneumonia with rapid onset fever, dyspnea, cough and sputum; may show lobar or diffuse infiltrates and neutrophilic leukocytosis; rusty sputum may occur.

diagnoses.name: COVID-19 pneumonia
diagnoses.description: Pneumonia with fever, cough, dyspnea and bilateral lung infiltrates; imaging may show peripheral and lower-zone ground glass opacities and/or consolidation.

diagnoses.name: Legionella pneumonia (Legionnaires’ pneumonia)
diagnoses.description: CAP that can have headache, abdominal pain, diarrhea and vomiting; may show hyponatremia and relative bradycardia as a characteristic feature.

diagnoses.name: Candidiasis of esophagus
diagnoses.description: HIV-related opportunistic infection (WHO stage 4 / AIDS-defining) involving candidiasis of the esophagus.

diagnoses.name: Cryptococcal meningitis
diagnoses.description: AIDS-defining condition; part of the opportunistic infections seen with advanced HIV (noted among conditions occurring at very low CD4 counts).

diagnoses.name: Typhoid fever
diagnoses.description: Systemic infection with features including relative bradycardia, mild hepatosplenomegaly and possible rose spots; labs may show leukopenia with relative lymphocytosis and absent eosinophils; blood culture is the gold standard.

diagnoses.name: Leptospirosis
diagnoses.description: Febrile illness in which chest radiograph may reveal patchy bronchopneumonia and small pleural effusion; ECG abnormalities can include bradycardia and nonspecific ST-T changes; LFTs may show raised AST/ALT and conjugated hyperbilirubinemia.

diagnoses.name: Chikungunya fever
diagnoses.description: Viral illness where a pruritic maculopapular rash (often trunk and limbs) may occur around day 2–3; adults are prone to migratory polyarthritis involving small joints of ankles, feet, hands and wrists.

precomputedExplanations.description: **Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP)** is an opportunistic fungal pneumonia that classically occurs in patients with impaired cellular immunity, especially untreated or advanced **HIV** with **CD4 <200 cells/µL**. It typically presents subacutely with fever, dry cough, and progressive dyspnea, often with hypoxemia out of proportion to chest examination and sometimes minimal early chest X-ray findings.
keySymptoms: **Subacute fever (~10 days)** - Suggests non-acute bacterial pneumonia; typical for opportunistic infections like **PJP**.
**Progressive dyspnea on exertion** - Hallmark of **PJP**, reflecting worsening diffusion impairment and increasing oxygen requirement.
**Nonproductive (dry) cough** - Common in **PJP** because alveoli are affected without purulent airway secretions.
**Retrosternal pleuritic chest pain** - Can occur with **PJP** due to pleural irritation or associated pneumothorax risk.
**Hypoxemia with increased (A–a) gradient** - Indicates impaired alveolar-capillary gas exchange, strongly supporting **PJP** physiology.
**Elevated LDH** - Nonspecific but frequently elevated in **PJP**, correlating with lung injury and inflammation.
**Normal or mild CXR changes early** - **PJP** may have minimal early radiographic findings despite significant hypoxemia.
**Bilateral perihilar diffuse interstitial pattern** - Classic chest X-ray pattern for **PJP** rather than lobar consolidation.
**CT ground-glass opacities with peripheral/basal sparing** - Typical CT signature for **PJP**, supporting an interstitial process.
precomputedExplanations.clinicalReasoning: The patient’s subacute course with fever, progressive exertional dyspnea, and dry cough is highly characteristic of **PJP** rather than typical bacterial pneumonia. Objective findings of **hypoxemia with an increased (A–a) gradient** indicate diffusion impairment, which aligns with **PJP** pathophysiology and often appears disproportionate to early physical signs. Imaging supports this: chest X-ray can be normal early or show bilateral perihilar interstitial infiltrates, while CT demonstrates patchy **ground-glass opacities** with relative peripheral/basal sparing. Given the strong association with immunosuppression, the presentation appropriately prompts **HIV testing** and evaluation for low **CD4** count.

**Imaging** - Leptospirosis may show alveolar hemorrhage/consolidation; **PJP** shows diffuse/patchy **ground-glass opacities** with typical distribution patterns.
**Laboratory clues** - Leptospirosis often has **bilirubin/creatinine elevation** and thrombocytopenia; **PJP** commonly has elevated **LDH** with hypoxemia and increased **A–a gradient**.
**Systemic features** - Leptospirosis frequently has **severe myalgias** and **conjunctival suffusion**; **PJP** often lacks these and presents primarily with respiratory compromise.
missingFindings: **Conjunctival suffusion** - Absence of this characteristic sign reduces likelihood of leptospirosis.
**Severe calf/lumbar myalgia** - Not described; its absence argues against classic leptospiral presentation.
**Jaundice** - No jaundice reported; severe leptospirosis commonly shows hepatic involvement.
**Acute kidney injury/oliguria** - No renal symptoms or AKI mentioned; renal involvement is a key leptospirosis clue.
**Exposure history** - No freshwater flooding, sewage, or animal urine exposure provided, which is central to leptospirosis risk.
**Hemoptysis/pulmonary hemorrhage** - Not described; leptospirosis respiratory failure often involves bleeding rather than isolated dry cough.

precomputedExplanations.description: Chikungunya fever is an acute arboviral illness transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes, classically causing abrupt fever and severe polyarthralgia. Respiratory involvement is not a defining feature, and progressive hypoxemic dyspnea with interstitial imaging patterns suggests an alternative diagnosis.
keySymptoms: **Acute high fever** - Sudden onset fever, often high-grade, typically begins abruptly after mosquito exposure.
**Severe polyarthralgia** - Prominent, disabling joint pains (often symmetric) affecting wrists, hands, ankles, and feet.
**Maculopapular rash** - Diffuse rash may appear after fever onset, commonly on trunk and limbs.
**Myalgia and fatigue** - Generalized body aches and marked tiredness are common during acute infection.
**Headache** - Frontal headache can occur, sometimes with photophobia, but usually without focal deficits.
precomputedExplanations.clinicalReasoning: This patient has subacute fever (~10 days) with progressively worsening **dyspnea**, **dry cough**, pleuritic retrosternal chest pain, and exertional breathlessness. Investigations show **hypoxemia with increased (A–a) gradient**, elevated **LDH**, and CT with **patchy ground-glass opacities** with peripheral and basal sparing—features that are highly characteristic of **Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP)**, especially in the setting of possible **HIV** with low **CD4 (<200)**. Chikungunya typically presents with abrupt fever and prominent **arthralgia** rather than progressive hypoxemic respiratory failure and classic interstitial CT findings.
precomputedExplanations.whyIncorrectForCase: Chikungunya fever does not typically cause progressive hypoxemic respiratory illness with diffuse **ground-glass opacities** and elevated **LDH**. The case lacks hallmark chikungunya features such as severe **polyarthralgia** and **rash**, while strongly matching **PJP** physiology and imaging.
keyDifferencesFromCorrect: **Primary syndrome** - Chikungunya is a febrile arthralgia illness; **PJP** is an opportunistic hypoxemic pneumonia.
**Respiratory pattern** - Chikungunya rarely causes progressive dyspnea; **PJP** causes subacute worsening dyspnea and dry cough.
**Imaging** - Chikungunya has no typical interstitial pattern; **PJP** often shows bilateral diffuse **ground-glass opacities** with characteristic distribution.
**Laboratory clue (LDH)** - LDH is not a classic chikungunya discriminator; elevated **LDH** supports **PJP** due to alveolar injury.
**Risk context** - Chikungunya depends on mosquito exposure/outbreak; **PJP** is linked to **immunosuppression** (e.g., untreated **HIV** with **CD4 <200**).
missingFindings: **Severe symmetric polyarthralgia/arthritis** - Its absence makes chikungunya much less likely than **PJP** here.
**Maculopapular rash** - Lack of rash reduces support for chikungunya in a febrile illness presentation.
**Epidemiologic exposure** - No mosquito/outbreak/travel exposure provided to support chikungunya acquisition.
**Typical course** - No abrupt onset with prominent joint symptoms; instead there is subacute progressive respiratory decline.
**Non-respiratory predominance** - Chikungunya usually has systemic/joint-dominant symptoms, not hypoxemic pneumonia.

differentialDiagnoses.name: Pulmonary tuberculosis (TB)
differentialDiagnoses.howToRuleOut: If symptoms have been present for several weeks or have failed to respond to standard antibiotics, consider TB and pursue microbiologic evaluation (e.g., AFB stain as part of sputum/BAL testing per listed investigations).
differentialDiagnoses.textbookReference: “When symptoms have been present for several weeks or have failed to respond to standard antibiotics, the possibility of TB should always be considered.”

differentialDiagnoses.name: Atypical pneumonia (e.g., Mycoplasma/Chlamydia/Legionella/viral)
differentialDiagnoses.howToRuleOut: Use the textbook’s clinical pattern (symptoms > signs, dry cough, no expectoration) and supportive labs (often low total WBC in viral/atypical). Chest X-ray patterns and targeted tests (PCR/serology listed for atypical pathogens) can support alternative atypical etiologies.
differentialDiagnoses.textbookReference: “Atypical… Symptoms > signs… Dry cough… No expectoration” and “In viral and atypical pneumonias, total leukocyte count is often <5,000/mm3” and “Oropharynx swab PCR for Mycoplasma pneumoniae and other atypical pathogens.”

differentialDiagnoses.name: Pneumococcal (lobar) pneumonia
differentialDiagnoses.howToRuleOut: Look for consolidation signs on exam and lobar homogeneous radiopacity with air bronchograms on chest X-ray; supportive tests include severe neutrophil leukocytosis and pneumococcal identification on Gram stain/culture/urinary antigen.
differentialDiagnoses.textbookReference: “Signs of consolidation…” and “Chest radiograph… homogeneous radiopaque with air bronchograms” and “Neutrophilic leukocytosis… suggests bacterial pneumonia” and “Gram’s staining… may show pneumococci… Urinary antigen…”

differentialDiagnoses.name: Hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP) / ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP)
differentialDiagnoses.howToRuleOut: Differentiate by clinical setting: onset after >48 hours of hospitalization (or after ventilation criteria) plus features such as purulent secretions and new infiltrate; this helps separate from community-onset pneumonia in an immunocompromised host.
differentialDiagnoses.textbookReference: “Hospital-acquired pneumonias… development of pneumonia after >48 hours of hospitalization.” and “At least two of three clinical features… and a new lung infiltrate.”

idealPathway.diagnosticApproach: From the textbook, approach this patient as pneumonia in an immunocompromised host because P. jirovecii is listed among causes in this setting and such cases have ‘symptoms more than the signs.’ Start with symptom-focused history (fever duration, progressive breathlessness, dry cough/no expectoration, pleuritic pain) and explicitly offer HIV testing. On examination, prioritize oxygen saturation (and assess for cyanosis/distress), vital signs (including confusion/delirium), and a focused chest exam for consolidation signs. Order investigations in a cost-effective sequence: CBC first (severity and bacterial vs atypical pattern), ABG when SaO2 <93% or severe features, HIV testing, then chest X-ray to confirm pneumonia and identify an interstitial/reticular pattern (noted for interstitial pneumonia including P. jirovecii). If prolonged symptoms or poor response suggests an alternative diagnosis such as TB, or if severe/unclear, proceed to further microbiologic confirmation using fiberoptic bronchoscopy with BAL and appropriate stains/cultures (including AFB stain) as listed in the textbook.
